rationale:
I skipped several of the strongest radar items because we covered them too recently. The MHRA fake-pen seizure and the photo study on compounded products were both in 10-17 S3. The SURMOUNT-5 stomach side effects were 10-17 S2. GLP-1 supplements were the 10-17 carousel. Reddit retatrutide reports were 10-16 S2. The orforglipron EU recommendation was in 10-17 L1 and S1. The retatrutide TRIUMPH-2 decoder was 09-30 L1. Response spread was the 09-29 carousel. I also kept the long-form clear of this week's fast-moving news.

**Long-form (L1).** This is a next-gen decoder in the "Did [new drug] beat tirzepatide?" format. It's the only long-form pattern that travels for us: EloraTZP has 373 views, while long-forms about approved drugs sit at a median of 4. I chose CagriSema because its trial program is published and checkable in depth: REDEFINE 1 and 2 in NEJM 2025, plus the REDEFINE 4 head-to-head with tirzepatide. That means the body rests on settled evidence and only the approval status needs dating.

**Shorts.**
- **S1:** a new head-to-head between two named drugs, tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and dulaglutide (Trulicity), on heart-failure events. It's emerging, with low competition, and it carries the exploratory caveat.
- **S2:** a spin-off of L1 as a dated status question. This format gave us our best Instagram Reel.
- **S3:** an evergreen tirzepatide (Zepbound) question on sleep apnea, with the CHEST 2026 news as the hook. I put the drug first and the brand in brackets, as the playbook recommends.

**Carousel (C1).** Carousels have reached 0–3 accounts every time, but the quota requires one, so this is a cheap, save-worthy myth-vs-fact list. Each myth on it was last covered on its own at least 5 days ago, and the list format is new.

**Mix.** Two emerging or rising pieces (S1, S2), two evergreen pieces with a timely hook (L1, S3) and one myth-buster (C1).

**Pillars.** Research ×2, beyond-weight ×2 and myths ×1.

**Body systems.** Weight and metabolism (L1, S2), heart (S1), breathing during sleep (S3) and mixed (C1).

**Suggested slots.** S3 (Zepbound, recognised brand, approved use) at 08:00, S1 at 13:00 and S2 at 20:00 as the riskier status test.

pieces.topic: CagriSema (cagrilintide + semaglutide), the amylin + GLP-1 combination: how it works and what the REDEFINE trial program showed, including the REDEFINE 4 head-to-head against tirzepatide
pieces.angle:
Hook (15 s or less): 'Did CagriSema beat tirzepatide? In the obesity head-to-head, no. In type 2 diabetes, the results were mixed.'

Then give REDEFINE 4 first: Novo Nordisk reported it as open-label, 809 adults with obesity, 84 weeks. Give both estimands, with each drug named next to its number: CagriSema 20.2% vs tirzepatide 15 mg 23.6% counting everyone, and 23.0% vs 25.5% if everyone stayed on treatment. Say it missed non-inferiority.

Add a short beat on the diabetes head-to-heads, credited to Novo Nordisk and dated:
- REIMAGINE 5 (Sep 2026): CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg 12.4% vs tirzepatide 5 mg 9.1% at 60 weeks. Lower doses on both sides.
- REIMAGINE 4: non-inferior on weight vs tirzepatide 15 mg, but missed on HbA1c.

Keep the planned beats on amylin, REDEFINE 1 and 2, non-inferiority, open-label design and side effects.

Status line, re-checked on publish day: 'As of [date], CagriSema is investigational. Novo Nordisk filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026. A filing isn't approval.'

Close with: 'Don't switch or stop on your own; talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.'

Title: 'Did CagriSema Beat Tirzepatide (Zepbound)? What the Head-to-Head Trials Found'.
pieces.working_title: Did CagriSema Beat Tirzepatide (Zepbound)? What the REDEFINE Trials Found
pieces.why:
Next-gen decoders are the only long-form format that travels for us (EloraTZP 373), and peer-reviewed NEJM trials make it verifiable in depth. The 09-28 Short only decoded a headline; this is the full deep-dive into the trial program. | fact-check: Good fit for the next-gen decoder lane, but the hook isn't accurate any more. 'In the only head-to-head obesity trial, no' leaves out two newer CagriSema vs tirzepatide trials in type 2 diabetes. In REIMAGINE 5 (Novo Nordisk press release, Sep 21, 2026), CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg gave 12.4% weight loss vs 9.1% on tirzepatide 5 mg at week 60, which Novo calls superior. In REIMAGINE 4, as reported in secondary coverage, CagriSema 2.4/2.4 mg was non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg on weight but missed non-inferiority on HbA1c. Saying 'no' with no qualifier would mislead.

REDEFINE 4 as reported by Novo Nordisk: open-label, 809 adults with obesity, 84 weeks. If everyone stayed on treatment, CagriSema 2.4/2.4 mg gave 23.0% vs 25.5% on tirzepatide 15 mg. Counting everyone regardless of adherence, it was 20.2% vs 23.6%. It missed the 3.2-point non-inferiority margin. Under our craft rules, the narration and the screen must show the count-everyone figure next to the on-treatment one. Label these numbers 'Novo Nordisk reported' unless a peer-reviewed paper exists at script time.

Status: Novo Nordisk filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in Q4 2026. Secondary sources say it's still unapproved as of about Oct 12, 2026. A decision could land near the publish date, so re-check the FDA and Novo Nordisk on the day.

REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 (NEJM 2025) are fine as planned. Copy the per-arm group sizes and the estimand from the papers.

Sources checked: Novo Nordisk REDEFINE 4 announcement via Investegate (https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/gnw/novo-nordisk-a-s-class-b--0qiu/novo-nordisk-a-s-cagrisema-demonstrated-23-/9442264); Drug Topics (https://www.drugtopics.com/view/cagrisema-did-not-meet-primary-end-point-of-noninferiority-to-tirzepatide); REIMAGINE 5 press release (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/21/3365319/0/en/novo-s-cagrisema-delivers-superior-weight-loss-versus-tirzepatide-in-reimagine-5-trial.html, which returned 403, so I confirmed it through search results only); REIMAGINE 4 listing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06221969).

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide vs dulaglutide in heart failure: exploratory SURPASS-CVOT analysis in adults with type 2 diabetes, heart disease and a history of heart failure
pieces.angle:
Title: 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs Dulaglutide (Trulicity) in Heart Failure: What Did the Trial Find?'

Answer by 10 s: 'An early signal, not proof. In adults with type 2 diabetes, heart disease and a history of heart failure, death or a heart-failure hospital visit happened in 18.2% on tirzepatide vs 21.5% on dulaglutide over about 4 years. Heart-failure hospital visits on their own were about the same.'

Then:
- Explain it's a post hoc look at SURPASS-CVOT (13,299 adults, so about 2,700 with heart failure; per-arm sizes from the EJPC paper). The comparison is dulaglutide, not placebo, and the authors call it hypothesis-generating.
- Status: as of Oct 2026, tirzepatide isn't FDA-approved to treat heart failure.
- One line on GI side effects.
- 'Don't switch or stop on your own.'
- Prescriber line.

On screen: 'post hoc analysis · SURPASS-CVOT · vs dulaglutide, not placebo · HF hospital visits alone: no clear difference'. Keep 'linked to' or 'associated with' language. 170 words or fewer, no emoji.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs Dulaglutide (Trulicity): Fewer Heart-Failure Events?
pieces.why:
Head-to-heads that name both drugs, with tirzepatide first, are our strongest YouTube pattern (SURMOUNT-5 147), and almost no creators have covered this yet. | fact-check: I confirmed the figures. The primary source is 'Outcomes in patients with diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and heart failure treated with tirzepatide or dulaglutide: SURPASS-CVOT analysis', European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, Oct 15, 2026. About 20.3% of the 13,299 participants (about 2,698 people) had a self-reported history of heart failure. Follow-up averaged about 4 years. All-cause death or heart-failure hospitalization/urgent visit: 18.2% on tirzepatide vs 21.5% on dulaglutide (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70–0.99). The authors call this composite post hoc, 'hypothesis generating' and 'nominal', with no adjustment for multiple comparisons.

The framing problem: the result is driven by death. All-cause death was 13.5% vs 16.7%. Heart-failure hospitalization or urgent visit alone did not differ (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.73–1.27, Healio/Endocrine Today, Jan 2026). CV death or HF events was HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.70–1.03), also not significant. A Heart Failure Reviews editorial called it 'a tie'. So the working title 'Fewer Heart-Failure Events?', and the line 'death or heart-failure events', imply something the analysis didn't show.

The angle also mixes up 'exploratory subgroup' and 'post hoc'. Here the subgroup was prespecified but the endpoint was post hoc.

Get the per-arm subgroup sizes from the EJPC paper itself. AJMC doesn't give them.

Sources checked: AJMC (https://www.ajmc.com/view/tirzepatide-linked-to-lower-death-or-hf-event-rates-in-t2d-hf, used only to locate the paper) and Healio (https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20260120/tirzepatide-heart-effects-do-not-vary-by-heart-failure-status).

pieces.topic: Is CagriSema approved yet? A dated status check on the amylin + semaglutide combination
pieces.angle: Spin-off of L1. Answer the status question in the first line, dated and credited to the FDA or Novo Nordisk (re-check at publish time). A filing, a committee view or an expected decision date is not approval. Then one line on what CagriSema is (semaglutide plus cagrilintide, an amylin analogue), plus one verified result with its trial, population and timeframe (REDEFINE 1, adults without diabetes, 68 weeks). Name the most common side effects (GI). Never suggest getting it outside a trial or prescription. Better route: ask your prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial. Say 'follow for more' unless L1 is already published. Prescriber line. 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: CagriSema (Semaglutide + Cagrilintide): Is It Approved Yet? (Oct 2026)
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 that drives traffic to the long video. Dated status questions about named drugs gave us our best Instagram Reel (84 reach).

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) for obstructive sleep apnea: what SURMOUNT-OSA showed, with the CHEST 2026 news as the hook
pieces.angle:
Answer by 10 s: 'Yes. Tirzepatide (as Zepbound) is FDA-approved, since December 2024, for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.'

Then:
- One AHI number at 52 weeks, tirzepatide vs placebo, from one named SURMOUNT-OSA trial (say whether it was the without-CPAP or with-CPAP trial), with per-arm group sizes from NEJM 2024.
- One line defining AHI: breathing pauses or shallow-breathing events per hour of sleep.
- Safety line: 'If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own; talk to your sleep clinician.'
- One GI side-effects line.
- One CHEST 2026 line: 'At the CHEST 2026 meeting, researchers presented early analyses linking GLP-1 medicines to wider heart and lung benefits in sleep apnea; these are early findings.'
- Prescriber line.

Don't compare GLP-1s with CPAP.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound): Can It Help Sleep Apnea?
pieces.why:
A plain 'Can it…?' question with the drug first and the brand in brackets about an approved use. It fits the proven YouTube pattern and Instagram's preference for yes/no questions, with a fresh hook from CHEST 2026 (Oct 17). | fact-check: The core claim checks out: the FDA approved Zepbound in December 2024 for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Name Zepbound specifically. Mounjaro isn't approved for sleep apnea, and the working title already uses Zepbound.

The CHEST 2026 items (Managed Healthcare Executive, Oct 17, 2026) were a systematic review of RCTs plus two retrospective TriNetX cohort studies about GLP-1s in general. These are conference abstracts and largely observational, so the one CHEST line needs 'linked to' language and a source credit, and it shouldn't be the evidence for the yes answer.

The angle's line 'it's used alongside CPAP, not as a replacement' isn't label wording. The OSA approval doesn't require CPAP. Recast it as a safety caveat instead (see the safer angle).

Copy the SURMOUNT-OSA AHI numbers, per-arm group sizes and the without-CPAP vs with-CPAP trial from NEJM 2024 (Malhotra et al.).

Source checked: Managed Healthcare Executive (https://www.managedhealthcareexecutive.com/view/more-pluses-for-glp-1s-for-obstructive-sleep-apnea-chest-2026).

pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide & Semaglutide: 5 Myths vs What the Trials Show
pieces.why:
Covers the myth-busting share of the mix with a list people save. Carousels reach only 0–3 accounts, so this is a low-cost format that reuses already-verified facts. | fact-check: The myths are accurate and safe, but it's a carousel, and all 19 carousels have reached 0–3 accounts. The playbook says to rebuild good carousel topics as Shorts or Reels, so consider moving this to a Short.

Scope fixes if it goes ahead:
- Myth 1: SELECT studied semaglutide only, in adults with heart disease and overweight or obesity without diabetes. Don't let the fact imply tirzepatide. Give the absolute rates (about 6.5% vs 8.0%) next to the roughly 20% relative reduction, copied from NEJM 2023.
- Myth 2: the SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy is tirzepatide only. Keep 124 vs 36 and 'about three-quarters fat', plus the kidney caveat and 'start gently'.
- Myth 3: give each trial average with its own drug and population, and don't merge STEP and SURMOUNT numbers.
- Myth 4: retatrutide is investigational as of Oct 2026. Credit the FDA warning about unapproved products, date it, and name no sellers.
- Myth 5: quote each drug's own label on GI effects during dose escalation, with no dosing.
